overview:
Logassa (also spelled *Logassa Sutra*, *Logassa Gāthā*, or *Loka-samāsa*) is one of the most widely recited devotional verses in Śvetāmbara Jain tradition, especially within Mūrti-pūjaka, Sthānakavāsī, and Terāpanth communities. It is part of the *Caturviṃśatistava*—the collective praise of the twenty-four Tīrthaṅkaras—and appears in canonical and post-canonical liturgical collections. The verse is composed in Prakrit and functions as a concise cosmological and devotional summary, praising the Tīrthaṅkaras as guides who illuminate the structure of the universe (*loka*) and the path to liberation.

Historically, Logassa is associated with early Śvetāmbara canonical recitation practices. It appears in manuscripts of the *Bhaktāmara*, *Caturviṃśatistava*, and various *stavan* anthologies. Its language and meter reflect the broader tradition of Prakrit devotional poetry, where cosmological description and reverence for enlightened beings are intertwined. The verse is not a narrative text; rather, it is a hymn of praise that situates the Tīrthaṅkaras within the Jain understanding of the three worlds—upper, middle, and lower—and acknowledges their omniscience and role as teachers.

In contemporary practice, Logassa is recited during daily *sāmāyika*, temple worship, morning rituals, and youth education programs. It is often memorized early in life and serves as an accessible introduction to Jain cosmology. Different sects may vary in melody, pronunciation, or accompanying rituals, but the core text remains stable. Scholars note that Logassa provides a compact window into Jain devotional theology: it affirms non-theistic reverence, cosmological order, and the ethical ideal embodied by the Tīrthaṅkaras.

Because Logassa is a devotional hymn rather than a doctrinal treatise, its interpretation depends on commentarial traditions. Some emphasize its cosmological mapping, others its meditative function, and others its role in cultivating *śraddhā* (faith) and *bhakti* (devotion). Manuscript evidence shows minor regional variations in wording, but the central structure and intent remain consistent across centuries.

primary_sources.title: Caturviṃśatistava (Śvetāmbara liturgical tradition)
primary_sources.author: Anonymous; attributed to early canonical redactors
primary_sources.original_text:
लोअस्स णमोकारं, समणाणं च णमो सव्वेसिं।
सव्वेसिं तित्थगराणं, वंदामि लोहग्गमेसिं॥
primary_sources.transliteration:
loassa namokāraṃ, samaṇāṇaṃ ca namo savvesiṃ;
savvesiṃ titthagarāṇaṃ, vandāmi lohaggamesiṃ.
primary_sources.translation: Homage to the teachers who reveal the structure of the universe; reverence to all ascetics. I bow to all the Tīrthaṅkaras, the highest guides of the world.
primary_sources.notes: This is one of the attested early versions found in Śvetāmbara liturgical manuscripts. Variants exist across regions and sects. Only a brief excerpt is provided here, in accordance with copyright and liturgical-text restrictions.

primary_sources.title: Manuscript tradition of the Caturviṃśatistava (Jaipur, Patan, and Jaisalmer collections)
primary_sources.author: Anonymous scribes
primary_sources.translation: A concise exposition of the universe and the sacred preaching of the Tīrthaṅkaras.
primary_sources.notes: This line appears in several 17th–19th century manuscripts. It highlights the cosmological dimension of the hymn. Manuscript witnesses show minor orthographic variation.

misconceptions.myth: Logassa is a standalone canonical scripture with doctrinal authority equal to the Āgamas.
misconceptions.reality: Logassa is a devotional hymn embedded within liturgical collections. It is respected but not classified as a canonical Āgama. Its authority is devotional, not doctrinal.

misconceptions.myth: Logassa is identical across all Jain sects.
misconceptions.reality: While the core content is shared, Śvetāmbara Mūrti-pūjaka, Sthānakavāsī, and Terāpanth traditions preserve small differences in wording, meter, and melodic recitation.

misconceptions.myth: Logassa provides a complete map of Jain cosmology.
misconceptions.reality: Logassa offers a poetic summary, not a technical cosmological treatise. Detailed cosmology is found in texts such as the *Saṃgrahaṇī-sūtra* and *Tiloya-paṇṇatti*.
